glossary.definition: An electric machine that moves heat from outdoor air into a building. It delivers several units of heat for each unit of electricity it uses.
Heat delivered divided by electricity used at one moment. It is higher on mild days and lower on cold days.
The COP averaged over a whole year. The model is tuned so each building's yearly SPF matches published Swiss field data.
Domestic hot water for showers and taps, as opposed to space heating. Heat pumps usually serve both.
A water tank that stores heat. Charging it early lets a home use the heat later, so the heat pump can run when electricity is cheap or the grid is quiet.
A price that depends on the hour: lower at night and on weekends, higher during the working day.
Power (kW) is how fast energy flows at one moment, like speed. Energy (kWh) is the total that has flowed, like distance. A bill is charged for energy; a grid is sized for power.
The largest power the district takes from the grid in any hour of the year. Grids and fuses are sized for it.
A controller that follows fixed rules, such as charging the tanks at night. The rules are written by hand and do not learn.
A way of letting software learn good control by trial and error against a score. It is planned for later phases and is not used yet.
How much CO2 is emitted per unit of electricity at a given hour. It is lower when hydro and nuclear dominate and higher when imports from fossil-heavy neighbours are needed.
Recorded by a real sensor or meter, such as a smart meter or a weather station.
Worked out from measured data with a stated formula, such as heat demand from heat-pump electricity.
Produced by a model rather than observed. The carbon curve is an example, so its level is an estimate.
Built for this study because no real data exists, such as the tank sizes and the apartment loads. Always shown hatched or labelled as assumed.
The reference CityLearn compares against: the same buildings without storage control. A value of one means no change from it; lower is better.

hero.question: Can smarter timing of heat pumps and hot-water tanks cut electricity cost and grid peaks in Swiss homes?
hero.context: Swiss homes are switching to [[heat pumps|heat_pump]], and heat pumps draw the most on cold winter evenings, exactly when the whole grid is busy. Electricity is cheaper at night under a [[time-of-use tariff|tou_tariff]], and a [[storage tank|storage_tank]] lets a home heat early and use the heat later. This project builds a realistic test bed to find out how much that timing can help.
hero.status: Phase A of 3 · the test bed is built and the first simple control rules are tested

steps.title: Real meter data
steps.text: Hourly electricity of the heat pumps and households, recorded in homes around Zurich.

steps.title: Heat demand
steps.text: Heat is not metered, so it is calculated from heat-pump electricity and outdoor temperature.

steps.title: A rule decides when to heat
steps.text: Simple rules decide when each home charges its heat and hot-water tanks. Smarter control comes later.

steps.title: The year is scored
steps.text: Each rule is judged on the electricity bill, the highest grid draw and the electricity bought, against doing nothing.

findings.title: What the first test shows
findings.verdict: The [[Night-charging rule|rule_based_control]] moves 2.9 percentage points of the year's electricity out of the expensive hours (from 40.0% to 37.1% of everything bought) and cuts the [[highest grid draw|peak]] by 6.1 %. But storing heat costs extra electricity: it buys 1.2 % more overall, so the bill does not fall. It rises by 0.5 %. The cheap-hour discount is small, 15.05 against 19.05 Rp/kWh.
findings.rules_line: The three tariff-timed variants land in the same range: the bill changes by +0.3 to +0.5 % and the highest grid draw by -5.2 to +1.2 % (a minus sign means a lower peak).
findings.chart_title: A cold winter weekday, hour by hour
findings.chart_caption: Grid draw of all the buildings together on Monday 2023-12-04, the coldest weekday of the year, with and without the night-charging rule. The shaded hours are the expensive tariff.
findings.tiles_caption: Whole-year totals compared with no control. Lower is better.
findings.closing: So timing alone, with simple rules, trims the peak but does not save money. That is why the next phases add smarter control and richer tariffs.

limitations.title: The CO₂ curve is an estimate
limitations.text: It is modeled from generation and trade data. Its level is about 61% to 62% of a published reference, so use it for timing, not for absolute values.

limitations.title: The tanks are assumed
limitations.text: No home has a documented tank, so the sizes follow a stated sizing rule and are tested at half and double size.

limitations.title: Comfort is not scored
limitations.text: The model has no indoor temperature, so heat demand is always met and comfort cannot be judged yet.
